subject: How Was My 1st Day in Germany?
body:
Hey Saiteja,

It was the 4th of November, 2021.

I took my first flight ever.

​
From Islamabad to Doha.

and then Doha to Berlin.

From the aeroplane window, I saw the beautiful city of Berlin
below.

Greenery. Super fast cars.

​
As the plane approached the ground, my heart started beating
faster.
​
Since I was a kid, I dreamed of coming to Europe, and now it was
all real.

​
I was quite happy that I finally made it.

But I was also worried at the same time.

I realized I was thousands of miles away from my family, my
friends, and my home.

Everything seemed strange and unfamiliar.

​
The streets were new, and the people around me were strangers.

​

At night, when I lay on my bed to sleep.

I felt the weight of my decision...

My first room in Germany
I had left everything behind to chase a dream.

* Home.
* Family.
* Friends.
* Everything.

​
For the first time, I felt truly alone.

I had a lot of responsibilities on my shoulders.

​

I started doubting myself on many things:

* What if it didn’t work out?
​
* What if I can't find a job here?
​
* What if I fail and have to go back to Pakistan?
​
* What if I had made the biggest mistake of my life?
​

I went to sleep, thinking the same and staring at the ceiling.

​
​

The next day, there was no one to wake me up.

I had to get up on my own, make my own breakfast, and had to
survive in this unfamiliar country by myself.

​
After spending a few days alone, I realized the true value of
family and what it really means to laugh with friends.

​

Well, coming to Germany was my own decision.

And there was no other choice than to survive here.

​
During my early days, all my doubts became true one by one.

* I faced a language barrier everywhere.
​
* I struggled to find permanent accommodation in Berlin.
​
* I tried for a field-related job but ended up being a food
delivery guy.

My first job in Germany
I don't consider any job to be low or small.

But, I hated doing this job.

It was not better than freelancing, which I was doing back home.

I felt like I was being unfair to myself.

​
I didn't come to Germany to deliver these pizzas and wine.

I didn't leave my homeland for this job.

I felt like a failure whenever I got ready for the food delivery
shift.

I didn’t tell any of my friends or family about it.

​

My first 6 months in Germany were the hardest because:

* I did not know German.
​
* I missed my family and friends.
​
* I had no connections in Germany.
​
* I had no permanent accommodation.
​
* I was doing a food delivery job even on cold, freezing nights.
​
​

I thought of giving up several times.

But then I asked myself:

* What would happen if I went back to Pakistan?
​
* How would my family feel about it?
​

Everyone will see me as a failed person, who couldn't survive
even in a most developed country, Germany.

These thoughts kept me going.

I also began to understand that

"What doesn’t kill you makes you stronger"

​

With all my courage, I chose to survive.

* I started learning German
​
* I started making new friends.
​
* I started applying for more field jobs.
​
* I started looking for more accommodations.

​
It took time, but I got through it, one by one.

​

Now, after 3 years in Germany, things have completely changed:

* I have a good job.
​
* I'm financially stronger.
​
* I have made new friends.
​
* I can support my family better.
​
* I'm able to help many students coming to Germany

​
I began to love this place.
​
I feel like coming to Germany was my best decision ever!

---------------------------
​
Was the struggles worth it?
---------------------------

Yes, it was all worth it. Each and every struggle was worth it.
​
​I'll choose Germany again if I am given a chance, even if I face
2x more troubles than before.
​
If you are coming to Germany, here is the best advice:

✅ Start learning German.

✅ Get ready for the initial hard days.

✅ Don't do odd jobs for the long term.

✅ Start searching for accommodation early.

✅ Find a good company of friends in Germany.

✅ Get some field experience before coming to Germany.

​

P.S.

If you're planning for Germany, you can take your first step
today by start learning German.

That is why I have created an Online German language course for

​

subject: The Day I Quit Germany
body:
Hey Saiteja,
​

Let me tell you a story.

When I was applying to Germany in 2021

I was this close to quitting my Germany dream.

​
​

I started my process in June 2021.

I shortlisted 7 universities for myself.

I applied to most of them just days before the deadline.

​
​And then I waited for months.

​
Every day, I checked my email, hoping for good news.

But one by one, I started receiving rejection emails.

First one… then another… then another.

​
​Out of 7 universities, 6 rejected me..

​
Each time I get rejected,

I felt tense and stuck.

I started to doubt myself.

“Maybe I will not get any admission.”

​

But that wasn’t the only problem…

Visa appointments were also uncertain.

Some students were waiting for months.

​

And I didn’t even know German.

Everything felt hard.

Germany started to feel impossible.

I still remember sitting alone and thinking:

“Maybe I should give up.”

But then, one day… an email came.

“You have been admitted to Berlin Hochschule für Technik.”

I read it again. And again.
​

After all the stress, waiting, and 6 rejections…

I finally got in.

That moment changed everything.

I was so happy 🥳
​

​

Here’s what I learned from that hard phase:

* Apply early.
​
* Apply to at least 10 universities.
​
* Rejections are normal
​
* Even when it feels impossible, keep going.

​

​

If you’re applying right now…

waiting for an admission or visa…

I know how it feels.

But don’t quit.

It only takes one acceptance to change everything.

​

Don’t give up.

Dreams take time.

But they’re worth it.

subject: Visa Rejection due to Study Gap?
body:
Hey Saiteja,

​

Are you interested in studying in Germany?

But have a study gap?

​
Today, I’m going to share with you:

* Can you get admission in public university with a study gap?
​
* Will your visa be rejected because of a study gap?
​
* How can you handle the study gap effectively?

***************************************
Can You Get Admission With a Study Gap?
***************************************

People say things like:

* Universities will reject you if you have a study gap
​
* The embassy will reject your visa
​
* Only X years gap is accepted

​
And so on and on…

​

But the truth is:

Getting admission with a study gap is not a problem.

Because you can get admission easily if you learn German.
​

Let me explain…
​

Here’s how learning German can help you:

-------------------------------
1) Increased Admission Chances:
-------------------------------

If you have German Proficiency:

* It shows commitment and dedication.
​
* You can apply to German-taught programs as well.
​
* German universities appreciate students who learn their
language.
​
* Your effort to learn German can help you stand out from other
applicants.

So, universities are more likely to consider your application,
even if you've a study gap.

​

--------------------
2) Less Competition:
--------------------

* Most international students apply to English-taught programs
only.
​
* This makes these courses very competitive.
​
* If you know German, you can also apply to German-taught
programs.
​
* They much less competition.

​
You can get admission there easily, even with a study gap.

​

--------------------------
3) Increased Visa Chances:
--------------------------

* The German embassy likes to see that you learned German.
​
* It shows you are serious about studying here.
​
* This makes them care less about your study gap.

*********************************************
How can you handle the study gap effectively?
*********************************************

Germany doesn’t have a fixed rule for how long a study gap can
be.

You can study again at any age.

But… you must have a good reason for your gap, such as:

* Learning a new skill.
​
* Getting work experience.
​
* Learning German.

​
When you apply, you can say in your motivation letter that you
used your gap to learn German.

When the visa officer asks, you can give the same answer.

********************************************
Will your visa be rejected with a study gap?
********************************************

If you learn German, your visa will NOT get rejected.

Because the university and embassy will see that you are ready
and serious.

So, learning German can help you stand out despite having a study
gap.

Need Help?
**********

We can handle 100% of your admission and visa process

subject: Growth doesn't happen at home
body:
There’s a strange comfort
in staying where everything already knows your name.

The same walls.
The same routines.
The same version of you…
repeating itself quietly.

Safe. Predictable. Still.

But nothing grows there.

Not courage.
Not clarity.
Not the person you keep imagining
you could become.

Growth asks for something uncomfortable.

It asks you to step outside—
not just physically,
but mentally.

To risk being seen as inexperienced.
To say things you’re not fully sure of yet.
To enter rooms where you are not the smartest one.

Because that’s where it begins.

Not in certainty—
but in exposure.

Every time you leave what’s familiar,
you create friction.

And friction shapes you.

It sharpens your thinking.
It reveals your blind spots.
It forces you to adapt.

And slowly…
you start becoming someone new.

Not because you tried to—
but because you had no other choice.

So if things feel uncomfortable right now,
if you feel slightly out of place,
if you’re questioning yourself more than usual…

Good.

You’re exactly where growth lives.

—
Bharat
